opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
Today's readings unsettled me.

I have always been drawn to humble people—people who are thankful despite hardship. There is something about them that immediately puts others at peace. Lately, though, I feel like I encounter fewer and fewer people like that. Whether that is actually true or simply how my heart now sees the world, I do not know. What I do know is that it is changing me.

I find myself becoming more impatient, more suspicious, and more hostile inside. Ironically, I often lack the confidence to express those feelings in the moment. Instead, they build quietly until I become someone I do not recognize.

Our business has been especially difficult lately. One client questions charges we have always billed for. Another is upset because of a misunderstanding in a text conversation. A big pool project has weighed heavily on me. Their concerns are not imaginary. They are right that some of our invoices lacked clarity, that work remained unfinished, and that our subcontractor created problems that became ours to own. I understand why they are frustrated.

Yet there is another side that is harder to explain.

Texts arrive late into the evening. Questions are repeated after months of notices. Communication is described as poor even when we have spent countless hours responding, documenting, and trying to solve problems. I begin to wonder if every effort we make will simply become another criticism. That feeling slowly hardens the heart.

Then I read St. Paul's words:

*"Always carrying about in the body the dying of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our body."*

I have read that passage before, but today it stopped me.

Perhaps the "dying" is not only physical suffering. Perhaps it is allowing my pride, my desire to be understood, my need to be appreciated, and my longing to be treated fairly to die over and over again. Not because those desires are wrong, but because if they become my measure of peace, they will eventually consume me.

Jesus did not say that serving others would be pleasant. He simply said that greatness is found there.

That is difficult for me.

Because I do not feel like a servant today. I feel tired. I feel misunderstood. I feel like every mistake overshadows every good intention. I want people to see the hours we spend solving problems before they ever become visible. I want them to believe that we genuinely care.

Instead, I often feel as though we stand accused.

Yet Paul continues by saying that this suffering allows the life of Christ to be made visible. That is the mystery. Christ is often seen most clearly not when everything goes well, but when we continue to respond with honesty, humility, and charity after we have been hurt.

The Psalm promises that those who sow in tears will reap with rejoicing.

Notice it does not say that tears are optional. They are part of the sowing.

Perhaps this season is teaching me something I have resisted my entire life: I cannot control how others receive my intentions. I cannot make someone trust me. I cannot make someone see the sacrifices we make.

What I can control is whether hardship slowly transforms me into a resentful person or into someone who resembles Christ just a little more.

That is the part I struggle with most.

Today I ask God for one grace—not easier clients, not fewer misunderstandings, but a heart that refuses to become hard. A heart that can acknowledge legitimate criticism without carrying bitterness. A heart that serves with truth instead of fear, sets healthy boundaries without anger, and remembers that every person I meet, including myself, is carrying burdens I cannot fully see.

If I lose that heart, then no successful business will matter.

If I keep it, then perhaps Christ's life is truly being manifested in my own mortal flesh.
